title: Cities Remember
thesis: A city map never records only the city that exists: it preserves demolished walls, monumental ambitions, property regimes and obsolete risks, allowing past urban orders to remain actionable long after the streets have changed.
whyThisSite: Terra Chartarum can place a rights-cleared historical town plan over a modern basemap, then connect the same city to bird’s-eye views, insurance sheets and catalogue records so continuity and erasure can be inspected rather than merely asserted.

claims.claim: The Severan marble plan measured about 18.1 by 13 metres, mapped architecture at approximately 1:240 and survives in 1,186 known fragments.
The Forma Urbis omitted political and sacred boundaries; even the Tiber appears through the blank between built edges, making architecture its principal urban memory system.
De’ Barbari’s six-block View of Venice constructs a comprehensive, inspectable civic image at monumental scale rather than reproducing one possible viewpoint.
The Agas map now supports a hyperlinked scholarly atlas of sixteenth- and seventeenth-century London, demonstrating how a historical city view becomes an index to place memory.
The Civitates Orbis Terrarum assembled hundreds of city plans and aerial views with descriptive texts, turning urban identity into a repeatable atlas genre.
Nolli’s 1748 Rome plan provides a high-resolution ichnographic surface suitable for a documented historical-to-modern georeferenced overlay.
Sanborn sheets selected construction, use and risk for insurance underwriting and were periodically revised, so their urban detail reflects a commercial purpose rather than total memory.
